prompt: Some people believe that the government should spend money on building train and subway lines to reduce traffic congestion. Others think that building more and wider roads is the better way to reduce traffic congestion. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
essay:
It is often argued that governments should invest in train and subway lines to reduce traffic congestion, while others believe that building more and wider roads would be more effective. Both views have some valid points. However, I personally favour greater investment in rail transport because it can reduce reliance on private vehicles and move large numbers of commuters efficiently.

On the one hand, I believe that governments should give greater priority to train and subway systems. One important advantage is that reliable rail services can reduce people's reliance on private vehicles. When commuters have a convenient alternative, they can travel to work without driving for the entire journey. For instance, an office worker living in a residential area could take a bus to a nearby station and complete the rest of the journey by subway. In this way, fewer cars would be needed on busy urban roads each day. Rail transport also has a much greater passenger-carrying capacity than private vehicles. A frequent subway service, for example, can move thousands of commuters through a busy city centre during peak hours. This can reduce pressure on roads and lower the demand for parking, making rail investment a useful long-term use of public funds.

On the other hand, some people consider road expansion a more practical solution. Giving vehicles additional space can improve traffic flow, particularly during busy periods. If a major two-lane road is widened to four lanes, for example, more vehicles can travel along it at the same time, which may shorten journeys in the short term. Wider roads are also necessary in smaller towns and locations without rail services because buses, delivery vehicles and emergency services depend on them. Nevertheless, this approach may have limitations in major cities. Easier driving can encourage more people to use private vehicles, so the initial improvement may gradually disappear as traffic increases. In some cases, congestion may simply shift to another road or junction rather than disappear completely. For this reason, road construction can be useful where rail transport is impractical, but it is less likely to provide a lasting solution to congestion in densely populated cities.

In conclusion, although wider roads can improve traffic flow in some locations, I believe that greater priority should be given to train and subway systems. Their ability to reduce private-car use and transport large numbers of commuters makes them a more sustainable approach to congestion, particularly in densely populated cities.
